They were awarded the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, along with Maurice [[term:Wilkins|term-00022]], who provided experimental proof of DNA’s structure. British chemist Rosalind [[term:Franklin|term-00023]] made invaluable contributions to this monumental achievement through her work in measuring X-ray diffraction images of DNA. Early in her career, Franklin’s research on the structure of coals proved helpful to the British war effort. After shifting her focus to biological systems in the early 1950s, Franklin and doctoral student Raymond Gosling discovered that DNA consists of two forms: a long, thin fiber formed when wet (type “B”) and a short, wide fiber formed when dried (type “A”). Her X-ray diffraction images of DNA ([[xref:CNX_Chem_10_06_RFranklin]]) provided the crucial information that allowed Watson and Crick to confirm that DNA forms a double helix, and to determine details of its size and structure. Franklin also conducted pioneering research on viruses and the RNA that contains their genetic information, uncovering new information that radically changed the body of knowledge in the field. After developing ovarian cancer, Franklin continued to work until her death in 1958 at age 37. Among many posthumous recognitions of her work, the Chicago Medical School of Finch University of Health Sciences changed its name to the Rosalind Franklin University of Medicine and Science in 2004, and adopted an image of her famous X-ray diffraction image of DNA as its official university logo.","is":"Uppgötvun Francis [[term:Crick|term-00020]] og James [[term:Watson|term-00021]] á byggingu DNA árið 1953 er eitt af stóru afrekunum í sögu vísindanna. Þeir hlutu Nóbelsverðlaunin í lífeðlis- eða læknisfræði árið 1962, ásamt Maurice [[term:Wilkins|term-00022]], sem lagði fram tilraunasönnun fyrir byggingu DNA. Breski efnafræðingurinn Rosalind [[term:Franklin|term-00023]] lagði ómetanlegt af mörkum til þessa stórafreks með vinnu sinni við að mæla röntgensveigjumyndir af DNA. Snemma á ferli sínum reyndust rannsóknir Franklin á byggingu kola gagnlegar fyrir stríðsrekstur Breta. Eftir að hafa fært áherslur sínar yfir á líffræðileg kerfi snemma á sjötta áratugnum uppgötvuðu Franklin og doktorsneminn Raymond Gosling að DNA samanstendur af tveimur formum: löngum, þunnum þræði sem myndast þegar hann er blautur (gerð „B“) og stuttum, breiðum þræði sem myndast þegar hann er þurrkaður (gerð „A“). Röntgensveigjumyndir hennar af DNA ([[xref:CNX_Chem_10_06_RFranklin]]) veittu þær mikilvægu upplýsingar sem gerðu Watson og Crick kleift að staðfesta að DNA myndar tvöfaldan gorm og að ákvarða smáatriði um stærð þess og byggingu. Franklin gerði einnig brautryðjandi rannsóknir á veirum og RNA sem inniheldur erfðaupplýsingar þeirra og afhjúpaði nýjar upplýsingar sem gjörbreyttu þekkingunni á þessu sviði. Eftir að hafa fengið krabbamein í eggjastokkum hélt Franklin áfram að vinna þar til hún lést árið 1958, 37 ára að aldri. Meðal margra viðurkenninga sem hún hefur hlotið eftir dauða sinn breytti Chicago Medical School of Finch University of Health Sciences nafni sínu í Rosalind Franklin University of Medicine and Science árið 2004 og tók upp mynd af frægri röntgensveigjumynd hennar af DNA sem opinbert merki háskólans."},{"key":"m68773:caption:CNX_Chem_10_06_RFranklin-caption","en":"This illustration shows an X-ray diffraction image similar to the one Franklin found in her research. (heimild: National Institutes of Health)"},{"key":"m68773:alt:fs-idp53384576-alt","en":"An image shows a circular illustration with rings of dots that are blurred together.","is":"Myndin sýnir hringlaga mynd með hringjum af punktum sem eru óskýrir."},{"key":"m68773:title:fs-idp26936448-title","en":"Key Concepts and Summary","is":"Lykilhugtök og samantekt"},{"key":"m68773:para:fs-idp129498528","en":"The structures of crystalline metals and simple ionic compounds can be described in terms of packing of spheres. Metal atoms can pack in hexagonal closest-packed structures, cubic closest-packed structures, body-centered structures, and simple cubic structures. The anions in simple ionic structures commonly adopt one of these structures, and the cations occupy the spaces remaining between the anions. Small cations usually occupy tetrahedral holes in a closest-packed array of anions. Larger cations usually occupy octahedral holes. Still larger cations can occupy cubic holes in a simple cubic array of anions. The structure of a solid can be described by indicating the size and shape of a unit cell and the contents of the cell. The type of structure and dimensions of the unit cell can be determined by X-ray diffraction measurements.","is":"Lýsa má byggingu kristallaðra málma og einfaldra jónaefnasambanda með tilliti til pökkunar kúlna. Málmatóm geta pakkast í sexstrendum þéttpökkuðum byggingum, rúmmiðjuðum þéttpökkuðum byggingum, miðjusettuðum byggingum og einföldum rúmmiðjuðum byggingum. Anjónir í einföldum jónabyggingum taka oft eina af þessum byggingum og katjónirnar fylla upp í rýmin sem eru á milli anjónanna. Litlar katjónir fylla venjulega upp í fjórflötungshol í þéttpökkuðu fylki anjóna. Stærri katjónir fylla venjulega upp í áttflötungshol. # Editing an Icelandic machine translation of a chemistry textbook (fable-editor, version 1)

You are editing the Icelandic machine translation of an English chemistry textbook (OpenStax _Chemistry 2e_),
which is being published as a free textbook for Icelandic upper-secondary students (aged about 16 to 20).
Work as an experienced Icelandic editor (yfirlesari) with a good knowledge of chemistry.

The goal is text a student can learn from: correct Icelandic in a register that is semi-academic but fluent
for younger readers. Judge grammar, agreement, word order and word choice in context, sentence by sentence and
across the passage. The translation must stay faithful to the English: do not add, drop or localize content
(units, examples and names stay as in the English), and do not explain more than the English does.

## What you receive

One JSON document (`"format": "fable-editor-user/1"`):

- `chapter` and `module`: where the text comes from.
- `englishContext`: the whole module in English, for context. Read it to understand the passage; edit only
  the `segments`.
- `terms`: the project's house terminology for this text. Each entry has the English forms (`en`) and the
  ruled Icelandic (`is`); `avoid` lists renderings known to be wrong for it. Use the ruled term, inflected as
  the sentence needs, wherever the English uses that term in that sense. Where no ruled term applies, choose
  the established Icelandic chemistry term.
- `segments`: in document order, each with a `key`, the English (`en`) and the machine translation (`is`).
  Segments are sentences, paragraphs, captions, list items, table cells or titles.

Both texts hold inline markers in double square brackets, such as `[[term:millikrafta|term-00001]]`,
`[[i:aq]]`, `[[sub:2]]`, `[[MATH:3]]`, `[[xref:CNX_Chem_10_01_KMTPhases1]]` or
`[[link:gagnvirku hermun|http://openstax.org/l/16phetvisual]]`. They carry formatting, formulas and
references. Keep every marker, with the same type and the same number of markers in the segment. You may edit
the Icelandic words inside a `term`, `link`, `i`, `b`, `em` or `u` marker, but never the part after `|`, and
never the contents of `MATH`, `MEDIA`, `TABLE`, `xref` or `docref` markers, or of `sub` and `sup` markers that
hold formula parts. You may move a marker within the segment when Icelandic word order needs it.

## What to return

Only the segments you change, each with its `key`, the whole edited Icelandic text of that segment, and one or
more tags saying what kind of change you made:

- `terminology`: a term changed to the house term or the established term;
- `grammar`: inflection, agreement, case, or another grammatical error;
- `fluency`: word order, phrasing or idiom, so the sentence reads as natural Icelandic;
- `meaning`: the translation said something the English does not;
- `register`: too formal, too colloquial, or too hard for the readers;
- `punctuation`: punctuation, capitals, spacing or number format.

Leave a segment out when it is already good. Each key appears at most once. Change only what improves the
text; a good machine-translated sentence does not need rewording.
